ratings.reason: An exact structural match: text and visual marks feed one request, with combination and channel switching explicitly supported. The mechanism is unusually rebuildable and broadly portable, though scribble-plus-text refinement is now a fairly expected design move.

Speech and parametrized gestures are explicitly fused for one modeling operation. The quote identifies the fusion pipeline but not its visible interaction details; the principle transfers well, although embodied 3D modeling entails specialized sensing.

A textbook exemplar: spoken intent and drawn reference marks jointly specify one command. The circle-and-say and brush-and-say examples expose both user action and system interpretation, making the mechanism directly reusable across visual workspaces.

Gaze, pointing, speech, and conversation history are fused to resolve a concrete referential breakdown. This materially expands usable speech interaction, though wearable AR hardware limits direct portability and the arbitration behavior is not fully described.

Images, color, and text are explicitly assembled into one GenAI prompt. The single-request structure is clear and highly transferable, although the quote does not explain weighting or conflict resolution and multimodal moodboards are not especially non-obvious.

Voice, text, and pointing may be used independently or together for dashboard onboarding, closely matching interchangeability without a stated mode change. Transfer is strong, but the quote lacks a concrete command example or an account of fusion and arbitration.

Vocal instructions and gestures are jointly interpreted for object manipulation, making the shared operation explicit. Deictic speech-plus-gesture is broadly useful, though its VR embodiment requires specialized hardware and is a relatively established multimodal move.

Point-and-click and natural language are two interchangeable channels for item selection. It is simple and portable, but the evidence does not establish fusion, mode-free switching, or a substantial outcome change; offering two selection methods is also conventional.

The quote establishes combined co-speech gesture and speech input, but gives no example of what a gesture contributes, what operation results, or how conflicts are resolved. Impact therefore cannot be judged strongly from the supplied evidence.

The cheaper-item example clearly shows speech and pointing composing one referential query. However, the quote is framed as a scenario rather than direct system behavior, so centrality, implementation, and demonstrated impact remain uncertain.

Hands-on shape manipulation and speech jointly convey intent for one generative-authoring operation. The complementary spatial and semantic roles are legible and interesting, although the swarm/shape-aware substrate narrows immediate transfer.

Real-time co-speech handwriting plausibly fuses spoken explanation with written mathematical work. The evidence does not specify the resulting request or system response, while tablet handwriting and linear-algebra tutoring constrain direct generalization.

Gaze and voice jointly perform physical-object selection, squarely matching a fused multimodal operation. The interaction is understandable from the quote, though the exact disambiguation behavior is absent and displayless smart glasses are specialized hardware.

Voice and pen input are both accepted as query channels and processed by one multimodal model. The quote does not clarify whether they are fused, interchangeable, or used for distinct query types, and the reported impact of the input design is unavailable.

Sketch and speech are integrated directly over an existing interface for context-aware LLM communication. The application-agnostic overlay makes this unusually transferable; a concrete end-to-end command example would be needed for maximum rebuildability.

Speech, grabbing, and movement are collected together and interpreted as narrative-play input. This is an interesting embodied fusion, but the quote describes an observation architecture rather than a discrete request, and XR play limits direct portability.

Facial-expression frames and message text are explicitly combined into one assistant input. The processing sequence is concrete and transferable to other affect-sensitive interactions, although outcome benefit in the high-stakes mental-health domain cannot be established from the supplied evidence.

Voice and binocular camera data feed one vision-language model, but the camera stream may be environmental context rather than a deliberate user-controlled channel. The quote does not identify a shared operation, arbitration behavior, or specific user outcome.

Semantic and graphical input are explicitly combined to express one initial exploration intent. The complementary channels are clear, but the quote does not define the controls, system response, or fusion logic, and the move is familiar in generative visual tools.

Rough sketches and text prompts jointly control a single image-generation operation, cleanly separating spatial and semantic specification. The pattern is highly reusable, though the evidence omits conflict handling and this pairing is increasingly standard.

Text and audio are used concurrently to search, modify, and create sounds, explicitly satisfying fused multimodal input. Reference media plus semantic language is a valuable transferable idea, although audio tooling makes the concrete implementation somewhat domain-specific.

Demonstrations and natural-language descriptions are accepted with an explicit and/or relationship, supporting both fusion and interchangeability for data-wrangling intent. It is broadly reusable, but the quote does not specify the demonstration channel or resulting behavior.

The user sketches an idea and voices design intent, plausibly creating one combined product-design request. The sequence is understandable, but the evidence does not explicitly confirm fusion, mode-free switching, or how the system aligns speech with sketch elements.

Images, voice, buttons, and dials contribute to one video-generation request in a clearly specified public appliance. The channel mix is concrete and accessibility-relevant, though the evidence does not say whether every channel is freely interchangeable and the installation context limits direct transfer.

Text, sketching, and region filling coexist in an iterative world-building workflow. The combination is portable, but the quote leaves open whether they feed the same request or operate as successive editing tools, so the strict structural signature is not fully demonstrated.

Voice and hand gestures support imaging operations where sterile interaction is a concrete, consequential need. The evidence does not show whether channels combine or substitute without mode changes, and the clinical AR setting and risk constraints reduce direct portability.

Text, sketches, and reference images can all contribute to character-image generation, a clear shared operation. The mechanism transfers readily to other generative media, but the quote does not explicitly state simultaneous fusion or channel arbitration.

A particularly legible dual-stream design: sketched frames control pacing while keyword-emoji input controls atmosphere in one comics-generation request. Assigning distinct semantic responsibilities to simultaneous channels is concrete and genuinely non-obvious, though tied somewhat to visual narrative structure.

Speech, sketching, and direct manipulation form an embodied mixed-reality creation interface. The quote establishes channel availability but not whether they are fused into individual requests, interchangeable without modes, or assigned to separate iterative steps.

Selected text, sketches, images, and story context are analyzed together to generate image-text cards, clearly demonstrating multi-source fusion. The mechanism is reconstructable at a high level, though the evidence does not explain selection controls, alignment, or arbitration among conflicting inputs.
